questions.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
questions.why: A vector has size and direction; velocity is speed in a stated direction.

questions.q: A stopwatch times 20 swings of a pendulum as 30.0 s. What is the period of one swing?
questions.why: Period = total time ÷ number of swings = 30.0 ÷ 20 = 1.5 s. Timing many swings reduces the reaction-time error.

questions.q: What does a micrometer screw gauge measure best?
o: The diameter of a thin wire
questions.why: It measures small lengths, such as a wire's diameter, to about 0.01 mm.

questions.q: Which is a scalar quantity?
questions.why: Temperature has size only, no direction.

questions.q: Two forces act on an object: 3.0 N to the east and 4.0 N to the north. What is the size of the resultant force?
questions.why: Forces are vectors, so at right angles they combine by Pythagoras: √(3.0² + 4.0²) = √25 = 5.0 N. Adding (7.0 N) or subtracting (1.0 N) ignores their directions.

long.q: A student wants to find the period of a simple pendulum, which is about 1 s, using a stopwatch. Describe how she should take her measurements to obtain an accurate value for the period.
scheme: B1: time a large number of complete oscillations, e.g. 20
B1: period = total time ÷ number of oscillations
B1: repeat the timing and calculate the average
B1: use a fixed reference mark at the centre of the swing and start/stop timing as the bob passes it (counting the first pass as zero)

long.q: An aircraft flies due north at 120 m/s relative to the air. A wind blows due east at 50 m/s. Calculate the size of the aircraft's resultant velocity and the angle between its direction of travel and due north.
scheme: A1: θ = 23° east of north (22.6°)

long.q: State the difference between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity. Then sort these quantities into scalars and vectors: distance, velocity, mass, acceleration, energy, force.
scheme: B1: a scalar has magnitude (size) only
B1: a vector has magnitude and direction
B1: vectors: velocity, acceleration, force (all three, no scalars included)
B1: scalars: distance, mass, energy (all three, no vectors included)

long.q: A student measures a stack of 200 sheets of paper with a ruler and finds it is 2.2 cm thick. Calculate the thickness of one sheet in mm, and explain why she measured a stack rather than a single sheet.
scheme: C1: thickness = 22 mm ÷ 200
B1: one sheet is too thin to measure with a ruler; measuring many sheets makes the reading larger so its (percentage) uncertainty is much smaller

long.q: Describe how a student can use a metre rule and two rectangular wooden blocks to measure the diameter of a ball as accurately as possible.
scheme: B1: place the ball between the two blocks with the blocks touching the ball on opposite sides, their faces parallel and perpendicular to the rule
B1: read the positions of the inner faces of both blocks on the rule, with the eye directly above each reading to avoid parallax
B1: diameter = difference between the two readings
B1: repeat with the ball turned to different orientations and take the average

questions.q: A car travels 120 m in 8.0 s at constant speed. What is its speed?
questions.why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 120 ÷ 8.0 = 15 m/s.

questions.q: On a speed–time graph, what does the area under the line give?
questions.why: Area under a speed–time graph = speed × time = distance travelled.

questions.q: A cyclist speeds up from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s. What is the acceleration?
questions.why: a = change in velocity ÷ time = (8 − 2) ÷ 3 = 2 m/s².

questions.q: A distance–time graph is a straight sloping line. What does this show?
questions.why: A constant gradient on a distance–time graph means constant speed.

questions.q: Near the Earth's surface and without air resistance, a falling object accelerates at about…
questions.why: The acceleration of free fall, g, is about 9.8 m/s².

questions.q: A space station orbits at 6800 km from the centre of the Earth. How far does it travel in one orbit?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates used the radius as the distance. One orbit is the circumference 2πr = 2π × 6800 ≈ 42 700 km.

questions.q: What does the area under a speed–time graph represent?
questions.why: Area under speed–time equals the product of speed and time, which gives the distance travelled.

long.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 5.0 m/s to 25 m/s in 8.0 s. Calculate its acceleration and the distance it travels in this time.
scheme: A1: a = 2.5 m/s²
C1: distance = average speed × time = 15 × 8.0

long.q: A cyclist's distance–time graph is a straight line from (0 s, 0 m) to (20 s, 100 m), then a horizontal line to (30 s, 100 m), then a straight line to (50 s, 300 m). Describe the motion in each of the three sections, giving speeds where possible, and calculate the average speed for the whole journey.
scheme: B1: 0–20 s: constant speed of 5.0 m/s
B1: 20–30 s: stationary (speed zero)
B1: 30–50 s: constant speed of 10 m/s (faster than the first section)
C1: average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 300 ÷ 50

long.q: A skydiver jumps from a hovering helicopter and falls for a long time before opening her parachute. Describe and explain how her velocity changes from the moment she jumps until she reaches terminal velocity.
scheme: B1: at first her acceleration is about 9.8 m/s² (g), because air resistance is zero and only her weight acts
B1: as her speed increases, air resistance increases
B1: so the resultant downward force decreases and her acceleration decreases
B1: when air resistance equals her weight, the resultant force is zero and she falls at constant (terminal) velocity

long.q: A train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 30 m/s in 40 s. It then travels at 30 m/s for 120 s, and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 60 s. Calculate the total distance travelled and the deceleration in the last part of the journey.
scheme: C1: distance while accelerating = area = ½ × 30 × 40 = 600 m
C1: distance at constant speed = 30 × 120 = 3600 m
C1: distance while decelerating = ½ × 30 × 60 = 900 m
A1: total distance = 5100 m
B1: deceleration = 30 ÷ 60 = 0.50 m/s²

long.q: A student wants to find the average speed of a trolley rolling down a long ramp, using a metre rule and a stopwatch. Describe how she should do the experiment and calculate the result, and suggest one way to make the timing more accurate.
scheme: B1: mark a start line and a finish line on the ramp and measure the distance between them with the metre rule
B1: release the trolley from rest at the start line and time it with the stopwatch until it crosses the finish line
B1: average speed = distance ÷ time
B1: repeat and take the average time, or use light gates and an electronic timer to remove reaction-time error

questions.q: What is the weight of a 5.0 kg mass where g = 9.8 N/kg?
An astronaut goes from the Earth to the Moon. What happens?
questions.why: Mass is the amount of matter and doesn't change; weight depends on the gravitational field strength, which is weaker on the Moon.

questions.q: Weight is measured in…
questions.why: Weight is a force, so its unit is the newton.

questions.q: What is gravitational field strength?
questions.why: Gravitational field strength g is the gravitational force on each kilogram of mass, measured in N/kg.

questions.q: A rock weighs 32 N on a planet where g = 4.0 N/kg. What is its mass?
questions.why: m = W ÷ g = 32 ÷ 4.0 = 8.0 kg. Using Earth's g (9.8 N/kg) gives the wrong answer, and multiplying or dividing the wrong way round gives the others.

long.q: An astronaut has a mass of 75 kg. Calculate his weight on Earth, where g = 9.8 N/kg. State his mass on the Moon and calculate his weight there, where g = 1.6 N/kg.
scheme: B1: mass on the Moon = 75 kg (mass does not change)
B1: weight on the Moon = 75 × 1.6 = 120 N

long.q: Explain the difference between mass and weight. In your answer give the unit of each.
scheme: B1: mass is a measure of the quantity of matter in an object (its resistance to a change in motion), measured in kg
B1: weight is the gravitational force acting on an object, measured in N
B1: an object's mass is the same everywhere, but its weight depends on the gravitational field strength where it is

long.q: Gravitational field strength g is the force per unit mass on an object in a gravitational field. Show that the unit N/kg is equivalent to m/s², and use F = ma to explain why, without air resistance, a heavy ball and a light ball dropped together reach the ground at the same time.
scheme: B1: 1 N = 1 kg m/s², so N/kg = (kg m/s²)/kg = m/s²
B1: the only force is the weight mg, so a = F ÷ m = mg ÷ m = g
B1: weight is proportional to mass, so the acceleration is the same (g) for both balls whatever their mass

long.q: A student hangs masses from 100 g to 500 g, in 100 g steps, on a newton meter and records the reading for each. Describe how she should use her results to show that weight is proportional to mass and to find a value for g.
scheme: B1: convert the masses to kg (0.10 kg to 0.50 kg)
B1: plot a graph of weight in N (y-axis) against mass in kg (x-axis)
B1: a straight line through the origin shows weight is proportional to mass
B1: g = gradient of the line (expected about 9.8 N/kg)

long.q: An object is weighed on Earth and then on the Moon, first with a beam balance (comparing it with standard masses) and then with a spring balance. Explain why the beam balance gives the same reading in both places but the spring balance does not.
scheme: B1: a beam balance compares the weight of the object with the weight of the standard masses
B1: on the Moon both weights decrease by the same factor, so the balance still balances with the same standard masses and shows the same mass
B1: a spring balance measures the force (weight) stretching the spring; the weight on the Moon is smaller, so the extension and the reading are smaller

questions.q: A block has mass 600 g and volume 200 cm³. What is its density?
questions.why: Density = mass ÷ volume = 600 ÷ 200 = 3.0 g/cm³.

questions.q: An object floats in water. What can you say about its density?
questions.why: Objects less dense than the liquid float in it.

questions.q: How do you find the volume of an irregular stone?
o: Lower it into a measuring cylinder of water and read the rise
questions.why: The volume of water displaced equals the stone's volume.

questions.q: Water (1.00 g/cm³), cooking oil (0.92 g/cm³) and glycerol (1.26 g/cm³) do not mix. They are poured into a tall jar and left to settle. Which liquid ends up on top?
questions.why: A less dense liquid floats on a denser one, so the layers settle in order of density with the least dense, the oil, at the top and glycerol at the bottom.

questions.q: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is the mass of an aluminium block of volume 20 cm³?
questions.why: m = ρ × V = 2.7 × 20 = 54 g. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 7.4 g or 0.14 g.

long.q: A stone of mass 240 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 50 cm³ to 146 cm³. Calculate the density of the stone.
scheme: C1: volume = 146 − 50 = 96 cm³
C1: density = 240 ÷ 96
A1: = 2.5 g/cm³

long.q: A rectangular block of gold measures 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 2.0 cm and has a mass of 772 g. Calculate the density of gold in g/cm³ and in kg/m³.
scheme: A1: density = 772 ÷ 40 = 19.3 g/cm³

long.q: Liquid A has density 0.80 g/cm³ and liquid B has density 1.2 g/cm³; they do not mix. Both are poured into a beaker and a small solid object C of density 1.0 g/cm³ is dropped in. Describe where A, B and C end up, and explain your answers.
scheme: B1: liquid A floats on top of liquid B, because A is less dense than B
B1: C sinks through liquid A, because C is denser than A
B1: C floats at the boundary, on top of liquid B, because C is less dense than B

long.q: Describe how to determine the density of cooking oil using an electronic balance and a measuring cylinder. Include how you would read the volume accurately.
scheme: B1: measure the mass of the empty, dry measuring cylinder
B1: pour in some oil and read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with the liquid surface
B1: measure the mass of the cylinder and oil, and subtract to find the mass of the oil
B1: density = mass of oil ÷ volume of oil

long.q: A fuel tank holds 0.050 m³ of petrol. The density of petrol is 720 kg/m³. Calculate the mass and the weight of the petrol. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
scheme: C1: mass = density × volume = 720 × 0.050
C1: weight = mg = 36 × 9.8

questions.q: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a 3.0 kg mass. What is its acceleration?
A spring stretches 2.0 cm with a 4.0 N load. Within its limit of proportionality, what load stretches it 5.0 cm?
questions.why: Extension is proportional to load: k = 4.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.0 N/cm, so 5.0 cm needs 10 N.

questions.q: A skydiver falls at terminal velocity. Which is true?
o: Weight is greater than air resistance
Air resistance is greater than weight
questions.why: At terminal velocity the forces balance, so there is no resultant force and no acceleration.

questions.q: A 4 N force acts 0.5 m from a pivot. What is the moment?
questions.why: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot = 4 × 0.5 = 2 N m.

questions.q: What keeps an object moving in a circle at constant speed?
o: A force along its direction of motion
A force away from the centre
questions.why: A force perpendicular to the motion, towards the centre, changes the direction but not the speed.

questions.q: A cyclist travels at a constant speed along a straight, level road. Which statement is correct?
o: The driving force is greater than the resistive forces
The driving force equals the resistive forces
There is no friction at all
Friction is smaller than the driving force but not zero
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a popular wrong answer said friction must be less than the driving force. Constant velocity means the resultant force is zero.

questions.q: An object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line. What can be deduced about the forces acting on it?
o: There are no forces acting on it
The forward force is greater than friction
The resultant force acting on the object is zero
questions.why: According to Newton's first law, an object continues at constant velocity when the resultant force is balanced (zero).

long.q: A spring has an unstretched length of 12.0 cm. With a load of 3.0 N hanging from it, its length is 16.5 cm. Calculate the spring constant, and the length of the spring when the load is 5.0 N. Assume the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
scheme: C1: extension = 16.5 − 12.0 = 4.5 cm
C1: extension with 5.0 N = 5.0 ÷ 0.67 = 7.5 cm

long.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a forward driving force of 3000 N acting on it. The total resistive force on it is 600 N. Calculate the acceleration of the car.
scheme: C1: resultant force = 3000 − 600 = 2400 N

long.q: A uniform metre rule of weight 1.0 N is balanced on a pivot at the 40 cm mark. A 3.0 N weight hangs at the 10 cm mark, and a force F acts vertically downwards at the 90 cm mark to keep the rule horizontal. State the principle of moments and calculate F.
scheme: B1: for an object in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point
C1: anticlockwise moment = 3.0 × 30 = 90 N cm
C1: clockwise moments = (1.0 × 10) + (F × 50), with the rule's weight acting at the 50 cm mark

long.q: A ball on a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Explain why the ball is accelerating even though its speed is constant, state the direction of the resultant force on it, and describe the ball's motion if the string breaks.
scheme: B1: the direction of motion keeps changing, so the velocity changes, so the ball is accelerating
B1: the resultant force (the tension) acts towards the centre of the circle
B1: this force is perpendicular to the ball's velocity, so it changes the direction but not the speed
B1: if the string breaks the ball moves off in a straight line along the tangent to the circle (ignoring gravity)

long.q: A racing car is designed to be very low and wide. Explain, in terms of centre of gravity, why this design makes the car less likely to topple over when it corners.
scheme: B1: being low gives the car a low centre of gravity
B1: being wide gives it a wide base
B1: so the car can tilt further before the line of action of its weight passes outside the base; until then the weight's moment turns the car back upright

questions.q: What is the momentum of a 2.0 kg ball moving at 3.0 m/s?
In a collision with no external forces, what is conserved?
questions.why: Total momentum is always conserved when no external force acts.

questions.q: Impulse is equal to…
questions.why: Impulse = FΔt, which equals the change in momentum.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. What is their speed just after the collision?
questions.why: Momentum is conserved: 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m/s before, shared by 3.0 kg after, so v = 6.0 ÷ 3.0 = 2.0 m/s.

questions.q: Why do crumple zones in a car reduce injuries in a crash?
o: They increase the time taken to stop, so the force is smaller for the same change in momentum
They reduce the change in momentum of the passengers
They increase the mass of the car
They reduce the car's speed before the crash
questions.why: Force = change in momentum ÷ time. The car still loses the same momentum, but crumpling makes it happen over a longer time, so the force on the passengers is smaller.

long.q: Trolley A of mass 2.0 kg moves at 3.0 m/s towards trolley B of mass 1.0 kg, which is at rest. They collide and stick together. Calculate their velocity just after the collision and the kinetic energy lost in the collision.
scheme: C1: momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m/s
C1: momentum after = (2.0 + 1.0) × v = 6.0
C1: kinetic energy before = ½ × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J and after = ½ × 3.0 × 2.0² = 6.0 J
A1: kinetic energy lost = 3.0 J

long.q: A tennis ball of mass 0.060 kg travels at 20 m/s towards a racket and leaves it at 30 m/s in the opposite direction. The ball is in contact with the racket for 0.0050 s. Calculate the impulse on the ball and the average force the racket exerts on it.
scheme: C1: change in velocity = 30 − (−20) = 50 m/s, so impulse = Δ(mv) = 0.060 × 50
A1: = 3.0 N s (kg m/s)
C1: F = impulse ÷ time = 3.0 ÷ 0.0050

long.q: In a crash, a car stops suddenly and an airbag inflates in front of the driver. Use ideas about momentum to explain how the airbag reduces the force on the driver.
scheme: B1: the driver's change in momentum (from moving to stopped) is the same with or without the airbag
B1: the airbag increases the time taken for the driver to stop
B1: force = change in momentum ÷ time, so a longer time means a smaller force on the driver

long.q: A rifle of mass 4.0 kg, initially at rest, fires a bullet of mass 0.010 kg horizontally at 400 m/s. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle.
scheme: B1: total momentum before firing is zero, so total momentum after is zero
A1: v = 1.0 m/s in the opposite direction to the bullet

long.q: Water leaves a hose horizontally at 12 m/s and hits a wall, stopping without bouncing back. 3.0 kg of water hits the wall each second. Calculate the force the water exerts on the wall.
scheme: B1: force = rate of change of momentum (change in momentum ÷ time)
C1: change in momentum each second = 3.0 × 12 = 36 kg m/s
A1: force = 36 N

questions.q: A 2.0 kg ball moves at 3.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
A 50 kg student climbs 4.0 m. What is the gain in gravitational potential energy? (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A motor does 600 J of work in 12 s. What is its power?
questions.why: Power = work done ÷ time = 600 ÷ 12 = 50 W.

questions.q: A lamp takes in 100 J and gives out 20 J as light. What is its efficiency?
questions.why: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100% = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.

questions.q: Which energy resource is renewable?
questions.why: Geothermal energy comes from heat inside the Earth and is not used up.

questions.q: Wind passes through a wind turbine and the blades turn. What happens to the air?
o: It speeds up and gains kinetic energy
It slows down because some of its kinetic energy is transferred to the turbine
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many thought the air speeds up. Energy taken by the turbine comes from the air's kinetic energy, so the air slows.

long.q: A student of mass 60 kg climbs a flight of stairs 3.0 m high in 4.0 s. Calculate the useful power developed. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
scheme: C1: work done = mgh = 60 × 9.8 × 3.0

long.q: A ball of mass 0.20 kg is dropped from a height of 5.0 m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate the gravitational potential energy it loses and its speed just before it hits the ground. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
scheme: B1: gravitational potential energy lost = kinetic energy gained

long.q: An electric motor with an input power of 500 W lifts a load of mass 40 kg through a height of 3.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the efficiency of the motor as a percentage. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
scheme: C1: useful work done = mgh = 40 × 9.8 × 3.0 = 1176 J
C1: useful output power = 1176 ÷ 4.0 = 294 W

long.q: A country is deciding whether to build a coal-fired power station or a wind farm. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
scheme: B1: coal advantage: reliable, produces electricity whenever needed / large output from one station
B1: coal disadvantage: non-renewable / burning it releases carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) or other pollution
B1: wind advantage: renewable / no fuel cost / no carbon dioxide released while generating
B1: wind disadvantage: output depends on the wind (unreliable) / many turbines over a large area are needed / noise or visual impact

long.q: Explain how the energy stored in coal originally came from the Sun, name two energy resources whose energy does not come from the Sun, and state the process that releases energy in the Sun.
scheme: B1: plants absorbed light from the Sun and stored the energy as chemical energy by photosynthesis
B1: the remains of the plants were buried and compressed over millions of years, forming coal, which still stores that chemical energy
B1: any two of: geothermal, nuclear (fission), tidal
B1: nuclear fusion (of hydrogen nuclei into helium)

questions.q: A 600 N force acts on 0.20 m². What is the pressure?
Why do snowshoes stop you sinking into snow?
o: They spread your weight over a larger area, reducing pressure
questions.why: Same force over a larger area gives a smaller pressure.

questions.q: What is the pressure due to 10 m of water? (density 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)
Why is a dam built much thicker at the bottom than at the top?
o: The water is colder at the bottom
To stop fish swimming under it
The pressure of the water increases with depth
questions.why: Pressure in a liquid = ρgh, so it increases with depth. The base of the dam must withstand the greatest pressure.

questions.q: A box of weight 120 N rests on a face measuring 0.30 m by 0.40 m. What pressure does it exert on the floor?
questions.why: Area = 0.30 × 0.40 = 0.12 m², so p = F ÷ A = 120 ÷ 0.12 = 1000 Pa. Using only one side as the area, or multiplying, gives the wrong values.

long.q: Calculate the pressure due to the water at a depth of 12 m. (Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)
A box weighing 600 N rests on the floor on a face measuring 0.50 m by 0.40 m. Calculate the pressure it exerts on the floor, and explain why a sharp knife cuts more easily than a blunt one.
scheme: C1: pressure = force ÷ area = 600 ÷ 0.20
B1: a sharp knife has a much smaller area of contact, so the same force gives a much greater pressure

long.q: A pressure gauge at the bottom of a storage tank shows that the pressure due to the oil in the tank is 5.0 × 10⁴ Pa. The density of the oil is 850 kg/m³. Calculate the depth of the oil. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
scheme: C1: Δp = ρgΔh

long.q: The wall of a dam is much thicker at the bottom than at the top. Explain why.
scheme: B1: pressure in a liquid increases with depth
B1: so the force of the water on each part of the wall is greatest at the bottom
B1: the wall is thickest at the bottom to withstand this greater force

long.q: A student lowers a pressure sensor into a tall cylinder of water and records the total pressure at depths from 0 to 0.50 m in steps of 0.10 m. Describe the graph she should plot and its expected shape, and explain how she can use it to find the density of water.
scheme: B1: plot pressure (y-axis) against depth (x-axis)
B1: a straight line with positive gradient that does not pass through the origin; the intercept on the pressure axis is atmospheric pressure
B1: gradient = ρg (since Δp = ρgΔh)
B1: density = gradient ÷ g (g = 9.8 N/kg), expected about 1000 kg/m³

questions.q: In which state are particles close together but able to move past each other?
questions.why: Liquid particles touch but can slide past one another.

questions.q: Gas in a sealed container is heated. Why does its pressure rise?
o: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
questions.why: Higher temperature means faster particles, so more frequent and harder collisions with the walls.

questions.q: A gas at constant temperature is squashed to half its volume. Its pressure…
questions.why: At constant temperature pV is constant, so halving V doubles p.

questions.q: What is absolute zero?
questions.why: −273 °C (0 K) is the temperature at which particles have the least possible kinetic energy.

questions.q: Why does evaporation cool the liquid left behind?
o: The fastest particles escape, lowering the average energy of those left
questions.why: The most energetic particles leave the surface, so the average kinetic energy, and the temperature, of the rest falls.

questions.q: Which describes the particles in a liquid?
o: They are far apart and move at high speed
They do not move at all
They are close together and move randomly
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some said particles in a liquid vibrate about fixed points; that describes a solid.

long.q: A gas has a volume of 200 cm³ at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. It is slowly compressed to 50 cm³ at constant temperature. State the relationship that applies and calculate the new pressure.
scheme: B1: pV = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature

long.q: A sealed metal can of air is heated, so its volume stays constant. Explain, in terms of particles, how the air exerts a pressure on the can and why this pressure increases as the air is heated.
scheme: B1: the particles move randomly at high speed and collide with the walls of the can
B1: each collision changes the particle's momentum and exerts a force on the wall; pressure is this force per unit area
B1: heating increases the average kinetic energy (speed) of the particles
B1: so they hit the walls more often and with greater force, so the pressure increases

long.q: Convert 27 °C and −196 °C to kelvin, and state what is meant by absolute zero.
scheme: B1: absolute zero (0 K, −273 °C) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles have the least possible kinetic energy

long.q: Smoke particles in air are viewed through a microscope. They are seen to move about in small, random, jerky steps. Explain this observation and state what it shows about air.
scheme: B1: the smoke particles are hit by air molecules, which are too small to be seen
B1: the air molecules are moving rapidly and randomly
B1: the collisions on different sides of a smoke particle are uneven, so it is pushed in a changing, random direction
B1: it shows air is made of tiny, fast-moving molecules (light, fast molecules can move much larger particles)

long.q: Describe the arrangement and the motion of the particles in a solid and in a gas.
scheme: B1: solid: particles are very close together in a regular arrangement (lattice)
B1: solid: particles vibrate about fixed positions
B1: gas: particles are far apart, with no regular arrangement
B1: gas: particles move randomly at high speed in all directions

questions.q: Why are gaps left between sections of railway track?
o: To allow for thermal expansion in hot weather
questions.why: Steel expands when heated; the gaps stop the rails buckling.

questions.q: How much energy raises 2.0 kg of water by 5.0 °C? (c = 4200 J/(kg °C))
While ice melts at 0 °C, its temperature…
questions.why: Energy goes into breaking the forces between particles, not raising the temperature.

questions.q: What is true of the particles of a substance at absolute zero?
o: They have the least gravitational potential energy
They have the least possible kinetic energy
They move faster than at any other temperature
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common misconception linked absolute zero to gravitational potential energy. It is the temperature of least kinetic energy.

questions.q: Why does the temperature of a liquid fall as it evaporates?
o: The more energetic particles escape from the surface, lowering the average kinetic energy of those left
The particles left behind lose mass
Evaporation only happens at the boiling point
Heat flows into the liquid from the air
questions.why: Only the fastest particles near the surface have enough energy to escape, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles, and so the temperature, falls.

long.q: Calculate the energy needed to heat 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg °C))

0.25 kg of ice at 0 °C is melted by a 500 W heater. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.3 × 10⁵ J/kg. Calculate the energy needed to melt the ice and the minimum time the heater takes to supply it.
State two differences between evaporation and boiling. Then explain, in terms of particles, why evaporation cools the liquid that is left behind.
scheme: B1: evaporation happens at any temperature, boiling only at the boiling point
B1: evaporation happens only at the surface, boiling throughout the liquid (with bubbles)
B1: the most energetic particles near the surface escape from the liquid
B1: so the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind decreases
B1: a lower average kinetic energy means a lower temperature, so the liquid cools

long.q: Describe an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of an aluminium block, using an electric heater, a joulemeter, a thermometer and a balance. Include the calculation and one precaution to improve accuracy.
scheme: B1: measure the mass of the block with the balance
B1: record the starting temperature, switch on the heater for a measured time, then record the highest temperature reached
B1: read the energy supplied from the joulemeter (or E = VIt)
B1: c = E ÷ (m × Δθ)
B1: precaution: wrap the block in insulation / put a drop of oil in the thermometer hole for good thermal contact

long.q: Railway lines are laid with small gaps between the lengths of rail. Explain why the gaps are needed, explain in terms of particles why the rails expand when heated, and state how the expansion of solids compares with that of liquids and gases for the same temperature rise.
scheme: B1: the rails expand in hot weather; the gaps let them expand without buckling
B1: when heated, the particles gain kinetic energy and vibrate with larger amplitude
B1: so on average the particles are further apart and the solid takes up more space
B1: solids expand least and gases expand most (liquids in between)

questions.q: How does thermal energy reach the Earth from the Sun?
questions.why: Space is a vacuum, so only radiation can carry energy across it.

questions.q: Which surface is the best emitter of infrared radiation?
questions.why: Dull black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers of infrared.

questions.q: Why is the heating element at the bottom of a kettle?
o: Hot water rises, setting up convection currents
questions.why: Heated water expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler water sinks to be heated.

questions.q: Why is a metal spoon a better conductor than a plastic one?
o: It has free electrons that carry energy
questions.why: Metals conduct well because delocalised electrons transfer energy quickly.

questions.q: Which outside surface keeps hot coffee in a cup warm for the longest?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many chose black. Shiny, light surfaces are poor emitters of infrared, so less thermal energy is lost.

long.q: Explain why metals are much better thermal conductors than non-metals such as glass.
scheme: B1: in all solids, energy is passed on by vibrating atoms (lattice vibrations) passing vibrations to their neighbours, which is slow
B1: metals also contain free (delocalised) electrons
B1: the free electrons gain kinetic energy at the hot end and move quickly through the metal, transferring energy by collisions further along

long.q: An electric heater stands on the floor at one side of a cold room. Explain how the whole room is heated by convection.
scheme: B1: air next to the heater is heated and expands
B1: its density decreases, so the warm air rises
B1: cooler, denser air sinks and moves in to take its place near the heater
B1: this sets up a convection current that circulates warm air around the room

long.q: Two identical cans, one painted dull black and one shiny silver, are filled with water at 80 °C and left to cool. Predict which cools faster and explain why. State two other factors that affect the rate at which a surface emits infrared radiation.
scheme: B1: the dull black can cools faster
B1: dull black surfaces are better emitters of infrared radiation than shiny silver ones
B1: surface temperature (a hotter surface emits at a greater rate)
B1: surface area (a larger area emits at a greater rate)

long.q: A vacuum flask keeps hot drinks hot. Explain how each of these features reduces thermal energy transfer: the vacuum between the double walls, the silvered surfaces of the walls, and the stopper.
scheme: B1: the vacuum has no particles, so it stops conduction and convection between the walls
B1: the silvered surfaces reflect infrared radiation back, reducing transfer by radiation
B1: the stopper is an insulator that stops convection currents (and evaporation) out of the top and reduces conduction

long.q: Explain how the average temperature of the Earth depends on the balance between the radiation it absorbs and the radiation it emits, and how an increase in greenhouse gases affects this.
scheme: B1: the Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun
B1: the Earth's surface emits infrared radiation
B1: the temperature stays constant when the rate of absorbing energy equals the rate of emitting energy
B1: more greenhouse gas absorbs more of the emitted infrared and returns some to the surface, so less is lost to space and the temperature rises until a new balance is reached

questions.q: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4.0 m. What is its speed?
Which wave is longitudinal?
questions.why: In sound the vibrations are parallel to the direction the wave travels.

questions.q: Water waves pass from deep to shallow water. What happens?
o: They slow down and their wavelength shortens
questions.why: Waves slow in shallow water; frequency stays the same, so wavelength decreases (refraction).

questions.q: Diffraction through a gap is greatest when the gap is…
o: about the same size as the wavelength
much smaller than the wave's amplitude
questions.why: Spreading is greatest when the gap width is similar to the wavelength.

questions.q: Which statement about water waves in a ripple tank is correct?
o: They carry water from one end of the tank to the other
questions.why: Examiners (2023): most candidates said water waves are longitudinal. The water moves up and down, at right angles to the direction the wave travels.

questions.q: Which wave property changes when a light ray refracts from air into glass?
o: Speed and wavelength both decrease while frequency remains constant
Frequency decreases while wavelength stays constant
questions.why: Frequency is determined by the source and does not change; in denser glass, light slows down so wavelength decreases (v = fλ).

long.q: In a ripple tank, 12 complete waves pass a fixed point in 4.0 s. The distance between five consecutive crests is 8.0 cm. Calculate the frequency, the wavelength and the speed of the waves.
scheme: B1: five consecutive crests are 4 wavelengths apart, so λ = 8.0 ÷ 4 = 2.0 cm

long.q: Describe the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each.
scheme: B1: transverse: the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction the wave (energy) travels
B1: example of transverse: light / any electromagnetic wave / water waves / seismic S-waves
B1: longitudinal: the vibrations are parallel to the direction the wave travels
B1: example of longitudinal: sound / seismic P-waves

long.q: Straight water waves of wavelength 1.5 cm in a ripple tank pass through a gap in a barrier. Describe and compare what happens to the waves after the gap when the gap is 1.5 cm wide and when it is 10 cm wide.
scheme: B1: the waves spread out after passing through the gap (diffraction)
B1: 1.5 cm gap (about one wavelength): strong spreading, with nearly circular wavefronts
B1: 10 cm gap (much wider than the wavelength): little spreading; wavefronts stay mostly straight, curving only at the edges
B1: the wavelength (and speed) is the same before and after the gap in both cases

long.q: Straight water waves travel from deep water into shallow water, with the wavefronts at an angle to the boundary. Describe what happens to the speed, wavelength, frequency and direction of the waves.
scheme: B1: speed decreases
B1: wavelength decreases
B1: frequency stays the same
B1: the waves change direction (refract), bending towards the normal

long.q: State what is meant by the amplitude, the wavelength and the frequency of a wave, and what is meant by a wavefront.
scheme: B1: amplitude: the maximum displacement from the rest (undisturbed) position
B1: wavelength: the distance between two neighbouring crests (or any two neighbouring corresponding points)
B1: frequency: the number of complete waves passing a point each second
B1: wavefront: a line joining neighbouring points on a wave that are in step, e.g. along a crest

questions.q: A ray hits a plane mirror at 30° to the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.why: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.

questions.q: Light enters glass at 40° to the normal and refracts to 25°. What is the refractive index? (sin 40° = 0.643, sin 25° = 0.423)
Total internal reflection can happen when light…
o: goes from glass into air at more than the critical angle
goes from glass into air at less than the critical angle
questions.why: It needs light travelling into a less dense medium at an angle bigger than the critical angle.

questions.q: What kind of image does a converging lens make of a distant object on a screen?
questions.why: An image you can catch on a screen is real; for a distant object it is inverted and diminished.

questions.q: A glass block has a refractive index of 1.5. What is the critical angle for light going from the glass into air?
questions.why: sin c = 1 ÷ n = 1 ÷ 1.5 = 0.667, so c = sin⁻¹ 0.667 ≈ 42°. 0.67 is the sine of the angle, not the angle itself.

long.q: Light passes from air into glass. The angle of incidence is 40° and the angle of refraction is 25°. Calculate the refractive index of the glass.
scheme: C1: n = sin i ÷ sin r

long.q: Glass has a refractive index of 1.50. State the two conditions needed for total internal reflection, and calculate the critical angle for glass.
scheme: B1: light must travel from glass towards air (from the medium with higher refractive index into the one with lower refractive index)
B1: the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle

long.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Describe three features of the image formed. Then state where an object must be placed for the lens to act as a magnifying glass, and describe that image.
scheme: B1: the image is real
B1: the image is inverted
B1: the image is diminished (smaller than the object)
B1: magnifying glass: object closer to the lens than the focal length (between the lens and F); the image is virtual, upright and enlarged

long.q: A narrow beam of white light passes through a triangular glass prism and a spectrum is seen on a screen. Explain why a spectrum forms, state which colour is refracted most, and state what is meant by monochromatic light.
scheme: B1: white light is a mixture of colours (frequencies), and glass refracts each colour by a different amount
B1: so the colours are separated into a spectrum (dispersion)
B1: violet is refracted most (red least)
B1: monochromatic light is light of a single frequency

long.q: Describe how a student can use a rectangular glass block, a ray box, a protractor and paper to investigate refraction, and how she can use her results to find the refractive index of the glass.
scheme: B1: place the block on paper, draw round it, and draw a normal where the ray will enter
B1: shine a ray at a measured angle of incidence i to the normal
B1: mark the ray leaving the block, join the entry and exit points to show the refracted ray, and measure the angle of refraction r
B1: repeat for several angles of incidence (e.g. 20° to 70°)
B1: plot sin i against sin r; the refractive index is the gradient of the straight line

questions.q: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has the shortest wavelength?
questions.why: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency.

questions.q: All electromagnetic waves travel in a vacuum at…
questions.why: All EM waves travel at the speed of light, 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, in a vacuum.

questions.q: Which is used in TV remote controls?
questions.why: Remote controls send short-range infrared signals.

questions.q: Which can damage skin cells and cause skin cancer?
questions.why: Ultraviolet radiation can damage cells in the skin.

questions.q: Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum is used for satellite television?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): infrared was a common wrong choice. Microwaves pass through the atmosphere to and from satellites.

questions.q: Which describes a digital signal?
o: A series of pulses with only two values, such as 1 and 0
A signal that can only travel through optical fibres
A signal that cannot be regenerated
questions.why: Examiners (2023): weaker candidates described digital signals as continuous. That is an analogue signal.

long.q: List the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency, and state one property that all electromagnetic waves share.
scheme: B1: radio waves, microwaves, infrared (in this order)
B1: then visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays (in this order)
B1: they all travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) / are all transverse

long.q: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 98 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves. (Speed of electromagnetic waves = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
Describe one harmful effect on people of each of: microwaves, ultraviolet radiation, and X-rays or gamma rays.
scheme: B1: microwaves: internal heating of body tissue
B1: ultraviolet: damage to surface cells and eyes, leading to skin cancer or eye conditions
B1: X-rays / gamma rays: mutation or damage to cells in the body, which can cause cancer

long.q: Mobile phones and satellite television both use microwaves. Give three properties of microwaves that make them suitable for these uses.
scheme: B1: they pass through the Earth's atmosphere (and ionosphere), so they can reach satellites
B1: they can penetrate some walls, so phones work indoors
B1: only short aerials are needed to send and receive them

long.q: Explain the difference between an analogue signal and a digital signal, and give two benefits of sending information as a digital signal.
scheme: B1: an analogue signal varies continuously and can take any value
B1: a digital signal has only two values (on/off, 1/0)
B1: noise can be removed when the signal is regenerated, so the signal keeps its quality over long distances (increased range)
B1: data can be sent at a higher rate

questions.q: What is the range of human hearing?
questions.why: Healthy young people hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

questions.q: Why can't sound travel through space?
o: There are no particles to vibrate
questions.why: Sound needs a medium; a vacuum has no particles to pass on the vibrations.

questions.q: An echo returns 2.0 s after a shout towards a cliff. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
questions.why: The sound travels there and back: distance = (340 × 2.0) ÷ 2 = 340 m.

questions.q: A louder sound has a larger…
questions.why: Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency.

questions.q: In a sound wave travelling through air, what is a rarefaction?
o: A region where the air particles are closer together, at higher pressure
The highest point of the wave
The point where the wave is reflected
A region where the air particles are further apart, at lower pressure
questions.why: Sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions (particles closer, higher pressure) and rarefactions (particles further apart, lower pressure). Crests belong to transverse waves.

long.q: A ship sends a pulse of ultrasound down to the seabed and detects the echo 0.40 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the sea.
scheme: C1: distance travelled by the pulse = 1500 × 0.40 = 600 m
B1: the pulse travels down and back, so the depth is half this distance
A1: depth = 300 m

long.q: Two students stand 200 m apart on a field. One bangs two cymbals together; the other starts a stopwatch on seeing the cymbals meet and stops it on hearing the sound. The time recorded is 0.60 s. Calculate the speed of sound, and suggest why this method is not very accurate and how it could be improved.
scheme: C1: speed = distance ÷ time = 200 ÷ 0.60
B1: the reaction time in starting and stopping the stopwatch is large compared with 0.60 s
B1: repeat many times and take the average time
B1: use a greater distance / swap positions and average to cancel the effect of wind

long.q: Explain how sound travels through air from a vibrating loudspeaker cone, and why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
scheme: B1: the vibrating cone pushes the air particles, which vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction the sound travels
B1: this produces a series of compressions and rarefactions that move away from the loudspeaker
B1: sound needs particles (a medium) to pass the vibrations on, and a vacuum has none

long.q: State how the pitch and the loudness of a sound are related to the properties of the sound wave, state the range of frequencies a healthy human can hear, and state what is meant by ultrasound.
scheme: B1: higher frequency gives a higher pitch
B1: larger amplitude gives a louder sound
B1: about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz)
B1: ultrasound is sound with a frequency above 20 kHz

long.q: The speed of sound is about 340 m/s in air, 1500 m/s in water and 5000 m/s in steel. State the general pattern shown by these values, and calculate the wavelength of a 2.5 kHz sound wave in steel.
scheme: B1: sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases

questions.q: Which material is magnetically soft, used in electromagnet cores?
questions.why: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily.

questions.q: What happens when two north poles are brought together?
questions.why: Like poles repel.

questions.q: Field lines around a bar magnet point…
o: from south to north outside the magnet
from north to south outside the magnet
questions.why: By convention, field lines go from north to south outside a magnet.

questions.q: How can you tell whether an iron-looking bar is a permanent magnet and not just a magnetic material?
o: Check that it attracts iron filings
Check whether it repels one pole of a known magnet
Check that it is attracted to a known magnet
questions.why: Both a magnet and an unmagnetised magnetic material are attracted to a magnet, but only a magnet can repel one, so repulsion is the reliable test.

questions.q: Where is the magnetic field around a bar magnet strongest?
o: Halfway along the side of the magnet
Near the poles, where the field lines are closest together
It is the same strength everywhere
questions.why: The closer together the field lines, the stronger the field, and they are most crowded near the poles.

long.q: Describe how to use a plotting compass to draw the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
scheme: B1: place the magnet on a sheet of paper and draw round it
B1: place the compass near one pole and mark a dot at the end the needle points to
B1: move the compass so the other end of its needle is over that dot, mark again, and repeat; join the dots to form a field line
B1: repeat from other starting points; add arrows from N to S in the direction the needle points

long.q: Compare the magnetic properties of soft iron and steel, and give one use of each that depends on these properties.
scheme: B1: soft iron is easily magnetised and easily loses its magnetism (a temporary magnet)
B1: steel is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism (a permanent magnet)
B1: soft iron use: the core of an electromagnet / transformer core / relay
B1: steel use: a permanent magnet, e.g. a compass needle or fridge magnet

long.q: An iron nail is held with one end close to the north pole of a bar magnet. The other end of the nail can now pick up steel paper clips. Explain why.
scheme: B1: the nail becomes magnetised by induction (an induced magnet)
B1: the end nearest the magnet's north pole becomes a south pole, so the nail is attracted to the magnet
B1: the far end becomes a north pole and induces magnetism in the paper clips, which are attracted to it

long.q: Two bar magnets are placed in a line with the north pole of one facing the south pole of the other, a short distance apart. Describe the magnetic field in the gap between them, and explain how the field-line pattern shows where the field is strongest.
scheme: B1: field lines go across the gap from the N pole to the S pole
B1: in the middle of the gap the lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced, so the field there is nearly uniform
B1: the field is strongest where the field lines are closest together

long.q: You are given a metal bar and a bar magnet. Describe how you could find out whether the bar is a permanent magnet, an unmagnetised magnetic material, or non-magnetic.
scheme: B1: bring one pole of the magnet up to each end of the bar in turn; if one end is repelled, the bar is a magnet (only repulsion proves this)
B1: if both ends are attracted by both poles, it is an unmagnetised magnetic material
B1: if there is no force on it, it is non-magnetic

questions.q: A current of 2.0 A flows for 30 s. How much charge passes?
A resistor has 6.0 V across it and 0.50 A through it. What is its resistance?
A 2.0 kW heater runs for 3.0 hours. How much energy does it use?
How does the resistance of a wire change if its length doubles?
questions.why: Resistance is proportional to length.

questions.q: The resistance of a thermistor as it gets hotter…
questions.why: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises.

questions.q: A current of 0.50 A flows through a lamp for 1 minute. How much charge passes through the lamp?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the most common error was not converting 1 minute to 60 s in Q = It. Q = 0.50 × 60 = 30 C.

questions.q: A wire is replaced by one of the same material and length but twice the diameter. What happens to its resistance?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought resistance is inversely proportional to diameter. R ∝ 1/area and area ∝ diameter², so doubling the diameter quarters R.

questions.q: A plastic rod becomes positively charged when rubbed with a cloth. Why?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought gaining electrons makes a rod positive. Only electrons move; losing negative charge leaves the rod positive.

questions.q: What is electric current defined as?
o: The work done per unit charge
The energy stored in a circuit
The rate of flow of electric charge (I = Q / t)
questions.why: Current in amperes is the rate at which charge in coulombs passes a point in the circuit per second.

long.q: A current of 0.40 A flows through a lamp for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes through the lamp.
A wire 2.0 m long with a cross-sectional area of 0.50 mm² has a resistance of 4.0 Ω. Calculate the resistance of a wire of the same material that is 3.0 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1.5 mm².
scheme: B1: resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area

long.q: Describe the shape of the current–voltage graph for a fixed resistor at constant temperature and for a filament lamp. Explain the shape of the graph for the lamp.
scheme: B1: fixed resistor: a straight line through the origin (current proportional to voltage, constant resistance)
B1: filament lamp: a curve whose gradient decreases as the voltage increases
B1: the lamp's resistance increases as the current increases
B1: because the filament gets hotter as the current increases

long.q: A 2.5 kW kettle is used for 6.0 minutes each day for 30 days. Electricity costs 20 cents per kilowatt-hour. Calculate the cost of using the kettle for the 30 days.
scheme: B1: 6.0 minutes = 0.10 h
C1: energy each day = 2.5 × 0.10 = 0.25 kWh
C1: energy for 30 days = 0.25 × 30 = 7.5 kWh

long.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain how the rod becomes charged, state the charge on the cloth, and describe what happens when the rod is brought near a second negatively charged rod hanging freely.
scheme: B1: friction transfers electrons (negative charge) from the cloth to the rod; positive charges do not move
B1: the rod gains extra electrons, so it becomes negative
B1: the cloth loses electrons, so it gains an equal positive charge
B1: the hanging rod is repelled (moves away), because like charges repel

questions.q: Resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.why: In series, resistances add: 4 + 6 = 10 Ω.

questions.q: Two 6 Ω resistors are in parallel. What is the combined resistance?
questions.why: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3, so R = 3 Ω. Parallel is always less than the smallest branch.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, what is the same across each branch?
questions.why: Each branch is connected across the same two points, so has the same p.d.

questions.q: A light-dependent resistor's resistance in bright light is…
questions.why: An LDR's resistance falls as light intensity increases.

questions.q: A 12 V supply is connected across a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor in series. What is the potential difference across the 8 Ω resistor?
questions.why: Total resistance = 12 Ω, so the current is 12 ÷ 12 = 1 A, and V = IR = 1 × 8 = 8 V. In series the p.d. divides in the ratio of the resistances (4 : 8).

long.q: Resistors of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω are connected in parallel to a 6.0 V supply. Calculate the combined resistance and the current from the supply.
A 12 V battery is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor and an 8.0 Ω resistor in series. Calculate the current in the circuit and the potential difference across the 8.0 Ω resistor.
scheme: C1: total resistance = 4.0 + 8.0 = 12 Ω

long.q: A potential divider is made from a 2.0 kΩ fixed resistor and a light-dependent resistor (LDR) in series across a 6.0 V supply. The output is the p.d. across the LDR. In the dark the LDR's resistance is 10 kΩ. Calculate the output voltage in the dark, and explain what happens to the output as the light gets brighter.
scheme: B1: in brighter light the LDR's resistance decreases
B1: so the LDR takes a smaller share of the 6.0 V and the output voltage decreases

long.q: The lamps in a house are connected in parallel, not in series. Give three advantages of this.
scheme: B1: each lamp can be switched on and off on its own
B1: if one lamp breaks, the others stay on
B1: each lamp gets the full supply voltage, so it lights at full brightness

long.q: A 6.0 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel pair of resistors, 4.0 Ω and 12 Ω, across a 9.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. Calculate the total resistance of the circuit and the current in the 4.0 Ω resistor.
scheme: A1: total resistance = 6.0 + 3.0 = 9.0 Ω
C1: current from supply = 9.0 ÷ 9.0 = 1.0 A
C1: p.d. across the parallel pair = 1.0 × 3.0 = 3.0 V
A1: current in 4.0 Ω = 3.0 ÷ 4.0 = 0.75 A

questions.q: What does a fuse do?
o: Melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too large
questions.why: It protects the cable from overheating by breaking the circuit when the current is too high.

questions.q: A kettle uses 2300 W on 230 V. Which fuse fits best?
questions.why: I = P ÷ V = 10 A, so use the next fuse rating above: 13 A.

questions.q: Why is a metal-cased appliance earthed?
o: So a fault sends a large current to earth and blows the fuse
questions.why: If the live wire touches the case, current flows to earth, the fuse blows and the case can't stay live.

questions.q: In a correctly wired mains plug and appliance, where are the fuse and the switch connected?
o: Switch in the neutral wire, fuse in the earth wire
Switch in the live wire, fuse in the earth wire
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some put them in the neutral or earth wire. Both go in the live wire so the appliance is isolated from the high voltage.

questions.q: Several high-power appliances are plugged into one extension lead. What is the main hazard?
o: The fuse in each appliance gets larger
The voltage of the mains supply rises
The current in the lead is too large, so the cable can overheat and start a fire
questions.why: The currents of all the appliances add up in the lead's cable. Too much current heats the cable, which can melt the insulation and cause a fire.

long.q: State three hazards of using mains electricity in the home.
scheme: B1: damaged (frayed or cracked) insulation exposing live wires
B1: overheating of cables when they carry too much current
B1: damp or wet conditions, e.g. water near sockets or switches / overloading sockets with too many appliances

long.q: A 2.0 kW heater is connected to a 230 V mains supply. Fuses rated at 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Calculate the normal current in the heater, and state and explain which fuse should be fitted.
scheme: B1: the 13 A fuse
B1: the 3 A and 5 A fuses would melt in normal use; 13 A is the lowest rating above the normal current

long.q: A metal-cased toaster has an earth wire and a fuse. A fault makes the live wire touch the metal case. Explain how the earth wire and fuse protect the user.
scheme: B1: the earth wire connects the metal case to earth
B1: a large current flows from the live wire through the case and earth wire to earth (a low-resistance path)
B1: this large current makes the fuse melt, breaking the circuit
B1: the case is no longer live, so a person touching it does not get an electric shock

long.q: A hair dryer has a plastic case and only two wires in its cable. Explain why it does not need an earth wire, and give one advantage of a circuit breaker over a fuse.
scheme: B1: it is double insulated: the outer case is an insulator
B1: so the case cannot become live even if a fault occurs inside, and no earth wire is needed
B1: a circuit breaker can be reset instead of replaced / it acts faster

long.q: Explain why the fuse and the switch in a mains circuit must be connected in the live wire and not in the neutral wire.
scheme: B1: with the fuse or switch in the live wire, the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage when the switch is off or the fuse melts
B1: if they were in the neutral wire, the appliance would still be connected to the live wire when switched off or after the fuse melted
B1: so someone touching a part inside the appliance could still get an electric shock

questions.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a meter. What happens?
o: An e.m.f. is induced while the magnet moves
A current flows only when the magnet is still
The coil becomes a permanent magnet
questions.why: A changing magnetic field through the coil induces an e.m.f.; no movement, no induced e.m.f.

questions.q: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 500 on the secondary. Input is 12 V a.c. What is the output?
questions.why: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = 12 × 500 ÷ 100 = 60 V (a step-up transformer).

questions.q: Why is electricity transmitted at very high voltage?
o: The current is smaller, so less energy is lost as heat in the cables
questions.why: For the same power, higher voltage means lower current, and cable losses depend on I²R.

questions.q: What does the split-ring commutator do in a d.c. motor?
o: Reverses the current in the coil every half turn
questions.why: Reversing the current each half turn keeps the coil turning the same way.

questions.q: A bar magnet is moved into a coil connected to a voltmeter. Which change gives the largest induced e.m.f.?
o: Moving the magnet in more slowly
Holding the magnet still inside the coil
Using a coil with fewer turns
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many thought slow movement induces more. The e.m.f. depends on how fast the magnetic field through the coil changes.

questions.q: Which statement about a step-up transformer is correct?
o: The primary coil has more turns than the secondary
An alternating current flows in the iron core
The secondary coil has more turns than the primary
It works with a steady direct current
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates mixed up the coils and thought current flows in the core. Step-up means Ns > Np; the core carries a changing magnetic field.

long.q: An ideal step-down transformer changes 230 V to 12 V. The primary coil has 1150 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil. When the secondary current is 2.0 A, calculate the current in the primary coil.
scheme: A1: = 60 turns
C1: Ip × 230 = 12 × 2.0 (power in = power out)

long.q: A power station sends 20 MW of power along cables at 400 kV. The total resistance of the cables is 5.0 Ω. Calculate the current in the cables and the power lost as heat in them, and explain why electricity is transmitted at a high voltage.
scheme: C1: P(lost) = I²R = 50² × 5.0
B1: a higher voltage means a smaller current for the same power, so much less energy is wasted as heat (I²R) in the cables

long.q: A coil is connected to a sensitive centre-zero meter. The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed into the coil, held still, then pulled out. Describe and explain what the meter shows, state two ways to get a larger reading, and state the magnetic pole at the end of the coil nearest the magnet as the magnet is pushed in.
scheme: B1: the needle deflects as the magnet moves in, because the changing magnetic field (field lines cut by the coil) induces an e.m.f. and a current
B1: no deflection while the magnet is held still
B1: deflection in the opposite direction when the magnet is pulled out
B1: any two of: move the magnet faster / use a stronger magnet / use a coil with more turns
B1: a north pole, because the induced current opposes the change that causes it (repels the approaching north pole)

long.q: Describe how a simple d.c. motor works, and state two ways of increasing the turning effect on its coil.
scheme: B1: the current-carrying coil sits in a magnetic field, so each side of the coil experiences a force
B1: the forces on the two sides act in opposite directions (one up, one down), producing a turning effect
B1: a split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn
B1: so the forces keep turning the coil in the same direction
B1: any two of: increase the current / use more turns on the coil / use a stronger magnet

long.q: A straight wire carrying a current lies at right angles to a magnetic field and a force acts on it. State the rule used to find the direction of the force, and describe what happens to the force when (i) the current is reversed, (ii) both the current and the field are reversed, (iii) the wire is turned to lie parallel to the field.
scheme: B1: Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force (motion)
B1: (i) the force reverses direction
B1: (ii) the force stays in the same direction
B1: (iii) there is no force

topics.name: The nuclear model of the atom

questions.q: A nucleus of carbon-14 has 6 protons. How many neutrons?
questions.why: Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number = 14 − 6 = 8.

questions.q: Isotopes of an element have the same number of…
questions.why: Isotopes have the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons.

questions.q: What did the alpha-scattering experiment show?
o: Most of an atom is empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
questions.why: Most alpha particles passed straight through; a few bounced back from a small, dense, positive centre.

questions.q: What did the alpha particle scattering experiment demonstrate about the atom?
o: The nucleus is tiny, positively charged, and contains most of the atom's mass
Electrons are embedded throughout a solid positive sphere
questions.why: Rutherford observed that most alpha particles pass straight through gold foil while a few deflect at large angles, proving a concentrated positive nucleus.

questions.q: Which describes nuclear fusion?
o: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
A heavy nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei
A nucleus emits an alpha particle
Electrons are captured into the nucleus
questions.why: Fusion joins light nuclei (as in the Sun) and releases energy. Splitting a heavy nucleus is fission, and emitting an alpha particle is radioactive decay.

long.q: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were fired at a thin sheet of gold foil. Describe the three main results and state what each tells us about the atom.
scheme: B1: most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space
B1: some were deflected, so the nucleus is positively charged (repels the positive alpha particles)
B1: a very small number were deflected through large angles, more than 90° (bounced back)
B1: so the nucleus is very small and contains most of the atom's mass

long.q: The nuclide notation for an atom of uranium is ²³⁵₉₂U. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of this nuclide.
scheme: B1: 92 protons
B1: 143 neutrons (235 − 92)
B1: 92 electrons

long.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon. Carbon has proton number 6. Explain what is meant by isotopes, using these two nuclides as the example.
scheme: B1: isotopes have the same number of protons, so they are the same element: both have 6 protons
B1: but different numbers of neutrons: carbon-12 has 6 and carbon-14 has 8
B1: so they have different nucleon numbers (12 and 14)

long.q: Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. Describe each process and state where each happens.
scheme: B1: fission: a large nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) splits into two smaller nuclei, usually after absorbing a neutron, releasing more neutrons
B1: fusion: two light nuclei (e.g. of hydrogen) join to form a heavier nucleus
B1: both processes release energy
B1: fission takes place in nuclear power stations; fusion takes place in stars such as the Sun

long.q: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Explain how a positive ion and a negative ion are formed from a neutral atom.
scheme: B1: the atom is neutral because the positive charge of the protons equals the negative charge of the electrons
B1: a positive ion forms when the atom loses one or more electrons
B1: a negative ion forms when the atom gains one or more electrons

questions.q: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
questions.why: Alpha particles are large and highly ionising, so they are stopped by paper or a few cm of air.

questions.q: A sample has a half-life of 3 days. What fraction is left after 9 days?
questions.why: 9 days is 3 half-lives: ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8.

questions.q: What is emitted in beta decay?
o: A fast-moving electron from the nucleus
questions.why: A neutron changes into a proton and a fast electron (beta particle) leaves the nucleus.

questions.q: Which is the most penetrating radiation?
questions.why: Gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.

questions.q: A counter reads 260 counts per minute near a source. The background count rate is 20 counts per minute. What is the count rate due to the source?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): weaker candidates forgot to subtract background, others added it. Source rate = measured − background.

long.q: A radioactive source has a half-life of 6 hours and an activity of 800 Bq. Calculate its activity after 24 hours.
scheme: C1: 24 h = 4 half-lives

long.q: Radium-226 (²²⁶₈₈Ra) decays by alpha emission to radon (Rn). Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) decays by beta emission to nitrogen (N). Write a balanced nuclide equation for each decay.
scheme: B1: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ...
B1: ... + ⁴₂α (⁴₂He), with nucleon and proton numbers balancing
B1: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ...
B1: ... + ⁰₋₁β (⁰₋₁e), with nucleon and proton numbers balancing
long.ans: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂α; ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁β

long.q: Compare alpha, beta and gamma radiation in terms of their ionising effect and their penetrating ability, and describe how each is deflected when it passes through a magnetic field.
scheme: B1: alpha: most strongly ionising, least penetrating; stopped by paper or a few cm of air
B1: beta: moderately ionising; stopped by a few mm of aluminium
B1: gamma: least ionising, most penetrating; only reduced by thick lead or concrete
B1: alpha and beta are deflected in opposite directions (beta more strongly); gamma is not deflected

long.q: A student uses a GM tube and counter to measure the count rate from a radioactive source. With no source present the count rate is 30 counts/min. With the source, the readings are 830 counts/min at the start, 430 counts/min after 4.0 minutes and 230 counts/min after 8.0 minutes. Determine the half-life of the source, and explain why the student should plot a graph rather than rely on single readings.
scheme: B1: subtract the background count rate of 30 counts/min from every reading
C1: corrected count rates are 800, 400 and 200 counts/min
A1: the count rate halves every 4.0 minutes, so the half-life is 4.0 min
B1: radioactive decay is random, so readings fluctuate; a smooth best-fit curve of corrected count rate against time gives a more reliable half-life

long.q: A factory makes paper. A radioactive source is placed on one side of the paper sheet and a detector on the other, to check the thickness. Explain why a beta source is used rather than an alpha or gamma source, and why the source should have a long half-life.
scheme: B1: alpha would be completely stopped by the paper, so no change in thickness would be detected
B1: gamma would pass through almost unaffected, so changes in thickness would make very little difference to the count
B1: beta is partly absorbed, so the count rate changes noticeably when the thickness changes
B1: a long half-life means the count rate does not fall noticeably through decay during use (and the source need not be replaced often)

questions.q: What causes day and night on Earth?
o: The Earth spinning on its axis
questions.why: One rotation of the Earth on its axis takes about 24 hours.

questions.q: What causes the seasons?
o: The Earth's changing distance from the Sun
The tilt of the Earth's axis
questions.why: The tilted axis means each hemisphere gets more direct sunlight for part of the year.

questions.q: Light from the Sun takes about 500 s to reach Earth. Light travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. How far is the Sun?
questions.why: distance = speed × time = 3.0 × 10⁸ × 500 = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m.

questions.q: How many stars are there in our Solar System?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some weaker candidates thought there are many. The Sun is the only star; the others are in our galaxy, not the Solar System.

questions.q: Why does the Moon appear to go through phases over about a month?
o: The Earth's shadow covers different amounts of it
Clouds block different parts of it
The Moon gives out different amounts of its own light
As it orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of its half that is lit by the Sun
questions.why: The Moon reflects sunlight and half of it is always lit. Its position in its orbit changes how much of that lit half faces us. The Earth's shadow only causes eclipses.

long.q: The Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m and takes 365 days to complete one orbit. Calculate the Earth's average orbital speed.
scheme: C1: distance in one orbit = 2πr = 2π × 1.5 × 10¹¹ = 9.4 × 10¹¹ m
C1: v = 2πr ÷ T

long.q: Explain why the Earth has day and night, and why it has seasons.
scheme: B1: the Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours
B1: the side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night
B1: the Earth's axis is tilted relative to its orbit around the Sun
B1: as the Earth orbits the Sun over a year, the hemisphere tilted towards the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days, so it has summer

long.q: The inner planets of the Solar System are small and rocky, while the outer planets are mostly large and gaseous. Use the accretion model of the Solar System's formation to explain this.
scheme: B1: the Solar System formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under gravity, forming the Sun at the centre
B1: in the disc around the Sun, particles collided and clumped together (accretion) to form planets
B1: close to the hot Sun only rocky and metallic materials could stay solid; the light gases were not held there, so inner planets are rocky
B1: further out it was cold enough for ices and gases to collect, so the outer planets grew large and gaseous

long.q: A comet moves around the Sun in a very elongated elliptical orbit. Describe and explain how the comet's speed changes during one orbit, using ideas about energy.
scheme: B1: the comet is fastest when it is closest to the Sun
B1: as it approaches the Sun, gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, so it speeds up
B1: as it moves away, kinetic energy is converted back into gravitational potential energy, so it slows down and is slowest at its furthest point
B1: the total of kinetic and gravitational potential energy stays constant

long.q: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape (show phases) over about a month.
scheme: B1: the Moon orbits the Earth about once a month
B1: the Moon does not give out light; the half facing the Sun is lit by reflected sunlight
B1: as the Moon orbits, we see different amounts of its lit half from Earth, so it seems to change shape

questions.q: What is a light-year?
o: The distance light travels in one year
The time for light to reach the Moon
questions.why: It is a distance: about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m.

questions.q: What is the evidence that the Universe is expanding?
o: Light from distant galaxies is redshifted
questions.why: Redshift shows galaxies moving away; the further away, the faster (and greater the redshift).

questions.q: What keeps a main-sequence star stable?
o: A balance between gravity inwards and pressure from fusion outwards
questions.why: Inward gravitational force is balanced by outward pressure from the energy released by fusion.

questions.q: What will a star like the Sun become at the end of its life?
o: A white dwarf (after a red giant)
questions.why: A low-mass star swells into a red giant, then its core is left as a white dwarf.

questions.q: Which sequence is correct for a star with about the same mass as the Sun?
o: Red giant → protostar → stable star → white dwarf
Protostar → stable star → red giant → planetary nebula and white dwarf
Protostar → red supergiant → supernova → black hole
White dwarf → red giant → stable star → protostar
questions.why: Examiners (2023): this recall question (syllabus 6.2.2) was mostly well answered; supernovae and black holes are for much more massive stars.

long.q: State what is meant by a light-year, and calculate its value in metres. (Speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s; 1 year = 365 days)
scheme: B1: the distance travelled by light in (a vacuum in) one year

long.q: Describe the life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun, from its formation to its end.
scheme: B1: a cloud of gas and dust (nebula) is pulled together by gravity to form a protostar
B1: it heats up until fusion of hydrogen begins; it becomes a stable star with the inward pull of gravity balanced by the outward pressure from the heat of fusion
B1: when most of the hydrogen in its core is used up, it expands to form a red supergiant
B1: it then explodes as a supernova
B1: the explosion throws out a nebula containing heavier elements, from which new stars and planets can form
B1: the core left behind becomes a neutron star, or a black hole if it is massive enough

long.q: Light from distant galaxies shows redshift. Explain what is meant by redshift and how observations of redshift support the Big Bang theory.
scheme: B1: redshift: the observed wavelength of light from a galaxy is longer than the wavelength emitted (shifted towards the red end of the spectrum)
B1: it shows that the galaxies are moving away from us
B1: more distant galaxies show a greater redshift, so they are moving away faster
B1: so the Universe is expanding, which suggests it began from a single very small, hot point (the Big Bang)

long.q: A galaxy at a distance of 2.0 × 10²⁴ m from Earth is moving away at 4.6 × 10⁶ m/s. Calculate the Hubble constant from these data, and use it to estimate the age of the Universe in years. (1 year = 3.2 × 10⁷ s)
scheme: A1: = 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second (s⁻¹)
C1: age ≈ 1 ÷ H₀ = 4.3 × 10¹⁷ s
A1: ≈ 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years

long.q: Describe the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) and explain why it is evidence for the Big Bang theory.
scheme: B1: microwave radiation of a particular frequency (wavelength) detected from all directions in space
B1: it was produced shortly after the Big Bang, when the Universe was very hot
B1: as the Universe expanded, this radiation was stretched to longer wavelengths (it cooled) and is now in the microwave region
